notes: Friday 2 Oct 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Thu 1 Oct U.S. close + overnight into Fri morning. NEW vs Thu 1 paper: U.S. stocks slight rebound as Treasury yields ease from multi-decade spike; Hormuz crude transit near prewar but refined fuels still tight; Micron record AI-memory quarter. Tech: California AG subpoenas OpenAI (replaces Gemini 4 Argon as lead); Micron/chip sentiment; Apple–OpenAI injunction hearing slip; session breadth notes. Politics: Kyiv drone/school/bridge strikes; senators press Taiwan arms delivery; Iran talks still stuck. Literature: Theo of Golden cross-list lock; CA indies John Green #1 + Steinem memoir; Borison/Picoult hot; Kuang/Dinniman/Lawhon slip some top-10s (Thoroughbreds/Dead Beat/Exit Party no longer the only frame). Social: fresh Nepal landslide deaths; Himlung avalanche; Ukrainian families still waiting; climate attribution debate continues.

stories.headline: U.S. stocks edge up as bond yields retreat from spike
stories.dek: S&P 500 +0.2% snaps a 3-day skid; Dow and Nasdaq barely green after wild Treasuries.
stories.caveman: On Thursday (Oct 1), Wall Street finished slightly higher. The S&P 500 rose about 0.2% to 7,666 and broke a three-day losing streak. The Dow closed at 50,926.56 (+0.04%) and the Nasdaq at 26,871.60 (+0.04%). Earlier, bond yields jumped and scared markets; later the selling in Treasuries cooled, so stocks could climb back. Europe had a rougher day, with big indexes down around 1–1.7%. Simple: U.S. stocks stopped falling, but nobody ran a victory lap.
stories.why_it_matters: When bond yields whip around, mortgage rates, company borrowing costs, and stock prices all shake.
stories.camps: Optimists say cooler yields + AI/chip strength can stabilize the tape. Caution camp says the week is still down and rate-cut hopes keep getting delayed.

terms.explain: Index of 500 big U.S. companies — a main scoreboard for U.S. stocks.
The interest rate on U.S. government bonds; when it jumps, risk assets often wobble.
Dow Jones Industrial Average — 30 large U.S. companies.
Several days in a row of closing lower.

stories.headline: Hormuz crude flows rebound — but diesel and gasoline stay tight
stories.dek: Tankers near prewar levels; damaged Gulf refining keeps fuel prices sticky.
stories.caveman: Fresh reporting on Oct 1 says crude oil moving through the Strait of Hormuz is largely back near prewar levels. That sounds like good news. The catch: refined fuels such as diesel and gasoline are still constrained because Gulf refineries were damaged or underfed, and some export limits elsewhere did not help. So the ‘black goo’ can leave, but the ‘ready-to-burn’ fuel is still scarce. Brent stayed elevated, around the low-$100s in recent sessions.
stories.why_it_matters: Drivers and shippers feel pump prices and freight costs even when crude headlines look calmer.
stories.camps: Relief camp focuses on crude transit recovery. Skeptic camp says the real inflation bite is in refined products until refineries fully recover.

terms.explain: Narrow sea lane by Iran/Gulf states that a huge share of world oil must pass through.
Unrefined oil pumped from the ground.
Fuel made from crude, like gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel.
A global oil price benchmark.

stories.image_alt: Oil tanker traffic near the Gulf

stories.headline: Micron posts record quarter on AI memory boom; peers rise, MU flat
stories.dek: Q4 revenue $54.23B; FY2027 guide strong — Wall Street still debating how much is priced in.
stories.caveman: Memory chipmaker Micron reported a record fiscal Q4: about $54.23 billion in revenue and $33.42 non-GAAP EPS. Full-year revenue hit about $133 billion. Bosses say AI demand is morphing into ‘super intelligence’ needs and they guided Q1 revenue around $61.5 billion. On Oct 1 trading, Nvidia/AMD/Intel got a sentiment bounce, but Micron’s own stock barely moved — because the bar was already sky high. Simple: memory is the hot grocery for AI, but the stock price already knew.
stories.why_it_matters: AI servers need mountains of memory; Micron’s numbers are a real-economy check on whether the boom is still shipping.
stories.camps: Bulls see multi-year supply tightness. Bears say margins and expectations leave little room for disappointment.

terms.explain: Earnings per share — profit divided by shares.
A company’s forecast for the next quarter.
Very fast memory chips used next to AI accelerators.
When a stock already reflects the good (or bad) news.

stories.headline: 10-year Treasury yield falls back after tagging a multi-decade high
stories.dek: Yield dropped toward ~5.21% after touching ~5.34%; stocks used the pause to climb.
stories.caveman: U.S. government borrowing costs went on a roller coaster. Reports said the 10-year Treasury yield had spiked to about 5.338% — talked about as a roughly 24-year high — then eased toward about 5.213% on Thursday as selling pressure cooled. That retreat helped stocks finish green. Simple: when lenders demand much higher interest to lend to the U.S., almost everything else gets more expensive and scarier.
stories.why_it_matters: The 10-year yield influences mortgages, car loans, and how investors value tech stocks.
stories.camps: Hawks say strong data keeps rates higher for longer. Doves hope the spike was an overshoot that markets can digest.

terms.explain: A U.S. government bond that matures in 10 years; its yield is a key rate benchmark.
The return bond buyers demand; higher yield = higher borrowing cost.
Someone who prefers higher rates to fight inflation.
Someone more willing to cut rates to support growth/jobs.

stories.image_alt: Global markets and bond trading mood

stories.headline: California AG subpoenas OpenAI over AI-related cyber incidents
stories.dek: Bonta seeks more records after model-misuse probes, including Hugging Face-linked concerns.
stories.caveman: On Oct 1, California Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office served an investigative subpoena on OpenAI. Officials want more information about cybersecurity incidents and risks tied to OpenAI models — including issues discussed around Hugging Face — and warned developers may face legal accountability if tools enable cyberattacks. Simple: the state is not just writing polite letters; it is demanding documents.
stories.why_it_matters: State probes can force safer defaults — or chill model releases — for the whole AI industry.
stories.camps: Safety advocates cheer oversight. Industry voices worry overlapping probes become politics-by-subpoena.

terms.explain: A legal order that forces a company to hand over documents or testimony.
A state’s top lawyer and law-enforcement officer for civil cases like this.
When people use an AI system to hack, scam, or cause other harm.
A popular platform for sharing AI models and tools.

stories.headline: Micron’s AI memory surge lifts chip sentiment — MU stock shrugs
stories.dek: Record results re-rate the memory story; Nvidia, AMD, Intel catch a bounce.
stories.caveman: After Micron’s monster print, traders on Oct 1 pushed other chip names higher even while Micron itself stayed roughly flat. Commentary framed memory supply as a bottleneck for AI systems through 2027–28. Simple: the industry party kept going; the host’s stock already arrived early.
stories.why_it_matters: Chip sentiment moves retirement accounts and Taiwan’s export cycle too.
stories.camps: Bulls call it confirmation of a multi-year AI hardware upcycle. Skeptics say valuations assume perfection.

terms.explain: DRAM/HBM/NAND parts that store data for computers and AI servers.
The market’s mood — fear or greed — often moving prices before facts change.
Room for a stock to rise if news is better than expected.
The slowest part of a system that limits everything else.

stories.headline: Apple–OpenAI trade-secrets fight: injunction hearing pushed to Oct 14
stories.dek: Apple wants device imaging and bans on alleged secret use; court continues the combined hearing.
stories.caveman: In federal court in San Jose, Apple’s trade-secrets case against OpenAI and related parties is still live. Coverage of the docket says Apple’s preliminary-injunction push — asking the court to block use of alleged secrets and preserve evidence — had a hearing window that slipped from around Oct 1 to Oct 14. Simple: Big Tech is fighting in court over people, files, and hardware know-how, not just chatbots.
stories.why_it_matters: Talent wars + secret recipes decide who ships the next devices and AI features.
stories.camps: Apple allies say poaching and file walks need hard brakes. Critics say injunctions can be used to intimidate rivals and ex-employees.

terms.explain: Valuable confidential business info, like a process or design not shared publicly.
A temporary court order that freezes behavior before the full trial ends.
Hiring away a rival’s employees to get skills or knowledge fast.
The court’s official list of filings and hearing dates.

stories.image_alt: Legal documents and technology dispute imagery
stories.image_credit: Photo: Book Riot (generic bookstore; article is court PDF)

stories.headline: AI and chip names help Wall Street climb after Micron’s record print
stories.dek: Oil & gas and industrials also led; Accenture spiked on its own headlines in the session tape.
stories.caveman: Market wrap notes from Oct 1 said gains in oil & gas, industrials, and utilities helped the tape, while AI/chip stocks got a lift after Micron. Some software names swung hard — Accenture was cited among top S&P gainers in one close report. Simple: tech did not carry the day alone, but silicon still set the mood music.
stories.why_it_matters: Breadth matters: a rally led by a few mega chips feels different from one with many sectors up.
stories.camps: Bulls like multi-sector green. Bears note Dow/Nasdaq barely moved and weekly performance is still negative.

terms.explain: How many stocks are rising versus falling — a health check for a rally.
Very large semiconductor companies that dominate indexes.
One trading day from open to close.
Electric/gas/water companies — often treated as steadier stocks.

stories.headline: Hormuz tankers near prewar levels as Gulf fuel bottleneck lingers
stories.dek: Crude transit recovers; geopolitics still price a risk premium into energy.
stories.caveman: EL PAÍS and other outlets reported Oct 1 that tanker trips through Hormuz are approaching prewar figures. Diplomats and markets still treat the Gulf as fragile because Iran-related tensions and damaged refining capacity have not fully normalized. Simple: more ships are moving, but politics can slam the door again.
stories.why_it_matters: Energy chokepoints sit at the crossing of war risk, inflation, and alliance politics.
stories.camps: De-escalation camp sees logistics healing. Hardliners say without a durable Iran deal the risk premium stays.

terms.explain: Extra price markets add when war or chaos seems possible.
A narrow place where traffic can be blocked easily.
Steps that lower the chance of fighting.
How much crude a region can turn into usable fuel.

stories.image_alt: Tankers in the Strait of Hormuz region

stories.headline: Russia hits Kyiv with drones — school shelter and Southern Bridge struck
stories.dek: Overnight wave of ~107 drones; energy grid attacks bring more blackouts.
stories.caveman: Ukrainian and international reports on Oct 1 describe a large Russian drone attack — about 107 drones overnight, with air defenses claiming most were shot down. Still, drones hit a Kyiv school area where students were sheltering and struck near the Southern Bridge, disrupting transit. Separately, strikes on energy infrastructure caused more power cuts as winter approaches. Simple: even ‘intercepted’ waves can wreck daily life.
stories.why_it_matters: Attacks on schools, bridges, and power are pressure tactics ahead of another cold season.
stories.camps: Ukraine and allies call it terror against civilians. Moscow frames strikes as hits on military-linked infrastructure — a claim Kyiv rejects.

terms.explain: Low-cost attack drones Russia has used in waves against Ukraine.
Missiles and guns meant to shoot down incoming drones and missiles.
When electricity goes out across a neighborhood or city.
Power, water, bridges, hospitals — systems life depends on.

stories.headline: U.S. senators press Trump to speed already-approved Taiwan arms
stories.dek: 21 Democrats cite $14B package delays after Trump–Xi meeting optics.
stories.caveman: Taipei Times reported a joint statement from 21 Democratic U.S. senators urging President Trump to immediately deliver congressionally approved defense aid and arms to Taiwan — including a roughly $14 billion package approved months earlier — after his meeting with China’s Xi Jinping. They argued support for Taiwan’s self-defense is ‘non-negotiable.’ Separately, Taiwan’s first new F-16V jets were due to arrive around Oct 2. Simple: Congress is yelling ‘ship the weapons already.’
stories.why_it_matters: Delivery speed affects Taiwan’s readiness and how Beijing reads U.S. commitment.
stories.camps: China hawks want faster deliveries. Restraint voices warn arms races and summit diplomacy need balance.

terms.explain: Government-approved deal to sell weapons to another country.
A country’s right to protect itself if attacked.
A public message signed by many lawmakers together.
The big region spanning the Indian and Pacific Oceans where U.S.–China rivalry is hottest.

stories.image_alt: Taiwan defense and F-16 related imagery

stories.headline: Iran talks still stalled as markets keep a Hormuz surcharge
stories.dek: Mediation continues, but sanctions-relief disputes block a clean off-ramp.
stories.caveman: Energy and diplomatic coverage into Oct 1 still describes U.S.–Iran talks as stuck, with mediators trying to find an off-ramp while neither side fully trusts the other on sanctions relief and regional security. That deadlock helps keep oil risk priced in even when tanker counts improve. Simple: phones are ringing, deals are not done.
stories.why_it_matters: No deal means higher odds of sudden shocks to fuel, shipping insurance, and alliances.
stories.camps: Diplomacy camp wants any credible ceasefire framework. Maximalist camps on each side demand the other blink first.

terms.explain: Penalties that block trade, banking, or travel to pressure a government.
A face-saving way to exit a crisis without more fighting.
A third party that tries to help rivals talk.
When talks stop moving because nobody will compromise.

stories.image_alt: Oil market and Middle East diplomacy

stories.headline: Book Riot chart mashup: Theo of Golden still unshakeable
stories.dek: Allen Levi’s novel hits all five major lists; several last-week fixtures fall out of the top 10.
stories.caveman: Book Riot’s Oct 1 roundup — combining NYT, Amazon, PW, USA Today, and Indie lists — says Theo of Golden by Allen Levi remains the rare title on all five. Grim Tidings (B.K. Borison) and Hollow Bones (Jodi Picoult) also show wide strength. Meanwhile Taipei Story, Dungeon Crawler Carl, and Pirate Queen slipped from some top-10 slots. Simple: one quiet novel keeps winning the popularity contest.
stories.why_it_matters: Cross-list staying power often predicts holiday inventory and book-club picks.
stories.camps: Indie booksellers celebrate sticky word-of-mouth. Diversity critics note the combined chart is still too white/male-skewed.

terms.explain: A ranking of what sold the most in a period, by one data source.
Sales ranking from independent bookstores.
People recommending a book to friends without big ads.
Appearing on several different bestseller charts at once.

stories.headline: California indies: John Green’s Hollywood, Ending debuts at #1 fiction
stories.dek: LA Times/CALIBA list also puts Mandel’s Exit Party at #2; Steinem memoir leads nonfiction.
stories.caveman: The California Independent Booksellers Alliance list for the week of Oct 4 (published Sept 30) crowns John Green’s Hollywood, Ending as #1 hardcover fiction. Emily St. John Mandel’s Exit Party sits at #2, with Marlon James, Ann Patchett, and Elizabeth Strout close behind. On hardcover nonfiction, Gloria Steinem’s An Unexpected Life opens at #1 over Charles Spencer’s Diana book and Ari Emanuel’s Roll the Calls. Simple: West Coast bookstores are buying big-name storytellers and big memoirs.
stories.why_it_matters: Regional indie charts often preview what becomes national book-club fuel.
stories.camps: Fans cheer star authors returning. Others want more midlist risk on the front tables.

terms.explain: California Independent Booksellers Alliance — organizes the state indie bestseller list.
A book with a stiff cover, usually the first expensive edition.
A true story from someone’s life, told by them (or with them).
The new/just-out titles stores push hardest.

stories.headline: Who’s hot: Grim Tidings & Hollow Bones widen their bestseller footprint
stories.dek: Borison’s paranormal romance and Picoult’s Hollow Bones show up across PW/USA Today/Indie stacks.
stories.caveman: Beyond the usual dark-academia chatter, Book Riot flags Grim Tidings by B.K. Borison and Hollow Bones by Jodi Picoult as multi-list winners this week. Seasonal vibes (fall, ghosts, secrets) are doing work. Simple: romance-with-bite and Picoult’s issue-driven fiction are both selling.
stories.why_it_matters: When romance and book-club fiction surge together, publishers reshuffle spring advances and marketing dollars.
stories.camps: Genre fans say the wall between ‘serious’ and ‘fun’ is fake. Traditionalists still separate literary prize bait from romance shelves.

terms.explain: Love stories with vampires, witches, ghosts, or other supernatural elements.
Novels designed for group discussion — big themes, talkable plots.
Campus stories with secrets, elites, and often murder.
Money a publisher pays an author before the book comes out.

stories.headline: Who’s not (as hot): Kuang, Dinniman, Lawhon slip some top-10 slots
stories.dek: Still selling — just not everywhere in the combined top tier this week.
stories.caveman: Book Riot notes that R.F. Kuang’s Taipei Story, Matt Dinniman’s Dungeon Crawler Carl, and Ariel Lawhon’s Pirate Queen got knocked out of some combined top-10 positions versus last week, even though they remain on overall lists. New seasonal titles crowded in. Simple: not a flop story — more like musical chairs on the podium.
stories.why_it_matters: A one-week slip can change bookstore display space even when absolute sales are still strong.
stories.camps: Authors’ fans shrug and point to long tails. Chart-watchers treat any drop as a narrative.

terms.explain: Steady sales over many months after the first big week.
Stories that use game stats/levels as part of the plot (Dungeon Crawler Carl’s lane).
The very top ranked slots people screenshot.
The front table or window where stores put books you notice first.

stories.headline: Nepal: new landslides kill at least 30 as monsoon misery continues
stories.dek: Trekkers stranded on Annapurna routes; country still reeling from earlier mega-floods.
stories.caveman: The Independent reports at least 30 people dead in fresh landslides and floods in Nepal on/around Oct 1, with climbers and trekkers forced to abandon routes or wait for helicopter rescues. The country is still recovering from an earlier catastrophic flood season. Simple: the ground keeps giving way, and rescue crews are exhausted.
stories.why_it_matters: Repeated disasters wipe out homes, farms, and tourism income — the cash many families need to rebuild.
stories.camps: Local officials plead for faster aid. Climate advocates tie the pattern to warmer air holding more rain.

terms.explain: When a hillside of mud/rock suddenly slides down.
Seasonal heavy rains in South Asia.
Mountain walking path used by tourists and guides.
Food, tents, medicine, and money sent to help disaster survivors.

stories.headline: Nepal avalanche/flood toll climbs; Himlung deaths add to grief
stories.dek: Watchers tally: floods/landslides ≥32 dead; Himlung avalanche toll reaches 11.
stories.caveman: Disaster monitors on Oct 1 tallied at least 32 dead from floods and landslides in Nepal, with a separate Himlung avalanche death toll reported at 11. Search teams dug through debris as weather stayed unstable. Simple: multiple mountains, multiple tragedies, one overwhelmed country.
stories.why_it_matters: Layered disasters make it harder to bury the dead, house the living, and keep clinics open.
stories.camps: Government spokespeople stress rescue first. Critics ask why early-warning guidance did not reach remote valleys faster.

terms.explain: A sudden slide of snow and ice down a mountain.
The counted number of people killed.
Alerts that tell people to move before a disaster hits.
A mountain community hard to reach by road.

stories.image_alt: Rescue teams searching after Nepal avalanche

stories.headline: A month on: Ukrainian families still wait for answers after Nepal–China floods
stories.dek: Dozens of Ukrainians among the missing; identification and repatriation remain slow.
stories.caveman: Reporting around Oct 1 says Ukrainian families are still desperate for information more than a month after deadly floods spanning Nepal–China border regions. Dozens of Ukrainian citizens were among those missing; relatives describe opaque updates and slow identification. Simple: disaster grief becomes worse when you cannot even confirm a goodbye.
stories.why_it_matters: Missing-persons limbo blocks funerals, insurance, custody, and mental recovery.
stories.camps: Families demand faster DNA ID and diplomacy. Officials cite destroyed roads and overwhelmed morgues.

terms.explain: Bringing a person’s remains (or a survivor) back to their home country.
Using genetic tests to confirm who a body is.
Someone not proven dead or alive after a disaster.
Aid from a country’s embassy/consulate to its citizens abroad.

stories.headline: Climate lens: scientists say warming helped uncork Nepal’s glacier disaster
stories.dek: Attribution work links thinner ice and thawing slopes to the earlier collapse — local geology still matters.
stories.caveman: Scientific coverage (Reuters/BBC earlier, still shaping Oct debate) finds climate change likely helped trigger Nepal’s catastrophic glacier/slope collapse by thinning ice and thawing mountain permafrost — though geology and past quakes also matter. Survivors and diplomats use that science in fights over who should pay for loss and damage. Simple: the mountain failed for many reasons; heat loaded the dice.
stories.why_it_matters: Attribution science is becoming a courtroom and COP bargaining chip for poorer nations.
stories.camps: Climate-justice voices want emitter funds. Opponents say local factors dominate and cash fights distract from adaptation.

terms.explain: Research that estimates how much climate change raised the odds of a disaster.
Ground that usually stays frozen; when it thaws, slopes can fail.
Money/help for irreversible climate harm already done.
The big annual UN climate negotiation meeting.
